source_refs.note: Tuning Musical Instruments: a main subheading of 7.9 Beats, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 158-161.

blocks.text: Here are some examples of how beats are generated in musical instruments:

items: Guitar: When playing two strings with slightly different tunings, beats are created. For example, playing a standard tuned string and a string tuned a few cents higher or lower.
Piano: Playing two keys white and black, adjacent to each other, creates beats.
Violin: When playing two strings with slightly different bow pressures or speeds, beats are generated.
Drums: When two drums with slightly different tunings are played simultaneously, beats are created.
Flute: When playing two notes with slightly different embouchure (lip and facial muscles) positions, beats are generated.
Organ: When playing two pipes with slightly different tunings, beats are created.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The sound produced by most of string and wind musical instruments is due to the formation of stationary waves or standing waves in these instruments.

items: Synthesizer: Generating two oscillators with slightly different frequencies creates beats.

blocks.text: In each of these examples, the slight difference in frequency between the two sound sources creates a periodic increase and decrease in amplitude, resulting in a "beat" or pulsation effect.

Musicians often use beats intentionally to create interesting rhythmic effects, add texture, or produce a sense of tension and release. However, in some cases, beats can be unwanted and may require adjustments to tuning, pitch, or playing technique to minimize their impact.

blocks.title: Example 7.7
blocks.problem: Two tuning forks exhibit beats at a beat frequency of 3 Hz. The frequency of one fork is 256 Hz. Its frequency is then lowered slightly by adding a bit of wax to one of its prongs. The two forks then exhibit a beat frequency of 1 Hz. Determine the frequency of the second tuning fork.
steps:
Frequency of first tuning fork = f₁ = 256 Hz
Beat frequency before loading = 3 Hz
Beat frequency after loading = 1 Hz
Frequency of second tuning fork = f₂ = ?

As   f₁ − f₂ = ±n
Then   f₂ = f₁ ± n

Putting values, we have
f₂ = 256 ± 3
Either   f₂ = 256 + 3;   or   f₂ = 256 − 3
f₂ = 259 Hz   or   253 Hz

Let us consider 259 Hz as correct answer (i.e., frequency of second tuning fork). When first fork is loaded with wax, the frequency of first fork must fall below 256 Hz i.e., 255, 254 and thus the number of beats produced per second will increase and will be greater than 3 beats. Since the number of beats per second decreases on loading first fork is one, therefore 259 Hz is not correct frequency of second tuning fork.
blocks.answer: Thus,   Correct frequency = f₂ = 253 Hz   ∵ 254 − 253 = 1 Hz

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: In 1711, F. J. Shore, who was a royal trumpeter and lutenist invented tuning forks.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The tuning fork was invented in 1711 by John Shore, the English royal trumpeter and lutenist.
